articles.title: The Rise of South African Football: Are We Becoming a Global Force?
articles.content:
South African football is in the middle of its biggest revival in twenty years. After years of heartbreak and missing major tournaments, Bafana Bafana has climbed back into the top 50 in the FIFA (International Federation of Association Football) rankings, while young local stars are finally earning moves to competitive European leagues.

Yet, while fans are excited, a big question remains: are we truly ready to become a regular force in world football, or is this just another temporary high?

How Hugo Broos Changed Bafana Bafana

The turning point for the national team started when Belgian coach Hugo Broos took charge. Instead of picking famous veteran names on reputation alone, Broos trusted hungry young players and built a united squad with clear tactical roles.

That bold plan paid off when South Africa claimed a bronze medal at the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON). Historic moments, like captain Ronwen Williams saving four penalties against Cape Verde and finishing 9th in the world at the prestigious Ballon d'Or Yashin Trophy, proved that local players can compete on the global stage under the South African Football Association (SAFA) banner.

The New Generation: Why European Scouts Are Watching

For years, very few South Africans played in top European competitions. Today, that picture is slowly shifting as teenage talent breaks through.

Wingers like Relebohile Mofokeng (who joined Belgian side Royale Union Saint-Gilloise) and Shandre Campbell (KV Kortrijk) are proving that early departures can fast-track development. Instead of waiting until age 25, these young players are testing themselves against European defenders while still in their late teens.

Belgium's Jupiler Pro League has become the favourite launchpad for South Africans, offering high-level coaching, European cup exposure, and a clear pathway toward top leagues in England, France, and Germany.

Why Do South African Players Struggle to Move to Europe?

If our country has so much raw football talent, why do only a few players secure contracts overseas each season? The answer comes down to three practical hurdles:

  • The PSL Comfort Trap: The Premier Soccer League (PSL), known officially as the Betway Premiership, pays top salaries by African standards. Star players can earn between R200,000 and R500,000 per month, which makes moving to a modest European club for lower net pay far less appealing.
  • High Transfer Valuations: Local clubs often demand over R40 million (€2 million to €3 million) for domestic talent. European scouts can easily find players in West Africa or South America with similar ability at half that price.
  • Work Permit Rules: Strict visa systems in countries like the United Kingdom require national teams to maintain high FIFA rankings before handing out automatic sports work permits.
Key Takeaway: Moving abroad before age 21 gives players the best chance to adapt to faster tactical decision-making, cold winter weather, and high-intensity pressing without the pressure of having to perform instantly.

Is the PSL Developing World-Class Talent?

The domestic league produces exceptional flair and exciting one-on-one dribblers. Continental success from clubs like Mamelodi Sundowns in the Confederation of African Football (CAF) Champions League proves that our top clubs have elite resources and deep squads.

However, the gap between domestic football and the international arena remains wide. In the PSL, matches often have a slower pace with lots of time on the ball, whereas modern international football demands intense physical pressing, rapid transition speed, and strict defensive shape.

Football Area Current South African Reality What Is Needed to Compete Globally
National Team Climbed into FIFA Top 50; strong AFCON results Consistent qualification for FIFA World Cup knockout rounds
Player Exports Small wave of talent in Belgium and England 5 to 10 regular starters in Europe's top 5 leagues
Domestic League Well-funded PSL, but dominated by one or two clubs Faster match tempo and greater tactical discipline across all 16 teams
Youth Academies Scattered private academies and school tournaments Standardized national grassroots coaching from age 10 onwards

What South Africa Needs to Stay at the Top

South Africa has the fan passion, stadium infrastructure, and athletic potential to lead the continent. To match the world-class winning standards set by South African rugby, football administrators must invest heavily in grassroots coaching from primary school age.

If local clubs continue encouraging young players to take European opportunities early, South African football will no longer just spark temporary excitement. It will cement our place as a genuine global force on the pitch.

articles.title: Bursaries Still Open for 2027 in South Africa
articles.content:
If you still need funding for university or college in 2027, you have not missed your chance yet. Several major South African bursaries are still accepting applications right now, but many close before the end of November and December.

Whether you are in matric or already studying at university, securing a bursary takes off the heavy burden of tuition, books, and living expenses. Here is the full list of bursaries that are still open, their exact closing dates, and how to apply before the doors shut.

Top Bursaries Still Open for 2027 Applications

Every year, thousands of students assume all bursary applications close in the middle of winter. In reality, some of South Africa's largest funding schemes accept applications right up to the start of the new academic year.

Here are the biggest bursary schemes you can still apply for today:

Bursary Programme Closing Date Who Can Apply What It Covers
NSFAS 2027 31 October 2026 Households earning under R350,000 / year Full tuition, accommodation, meals, book allowance
ISFAP Missing Middle 31 October 2026 Households earning R350,000 – R600,000 / year Full tuition, residence, food, personal allowance
Funza Lushaka (Returning) 30 November 2026 Returning B.Ed and PGCE teaching students Tuition, accommodation, study material
DSTI-NRF Honours Funding 23 November 2026 Postgraduate Honours (Science & Humanities) Full-cost or partial-cost study support
Milpark Bursary Programme 10 December 2026 Commerce, banking, and business students Tuition and examination fees
PSG Bursary Programme 20 December 2026 IT, Finance, Actuarial Science, Engineering Tuition, textbooks, and mentoring
Funza Lushaka (New Students) 31 January 2027 First-year teaching students (priority subjects) Comprehensive tuition, meals, and living allowance
Urgent Deadline Alert: Both NSFAS and ISFAP close on 31 October 2026. If you have not submitted your online application yet, do it today to ensure your household income documents are verified in time.

1. Government Funding: NSFAS and ISFAP

The official NSFAS portal handles government funding for students from low-income families. If your combined household income is R350,000 or less per year, NSFAS pays your full university fees, accommodation, and monthly food allowance.

If your family earns slightly too much for NSFAS—between R350,000 and R600,000 annually—you qualify as "missing middle." The Ikusasa Student Financial Aid Programme (ISFAP) was built specifically to fund these students in high-demand fields like medicine, engineering, and accounting.

2. Teaching Bursaries: Funza Lushaka

If you plan to study education, the Funza Lushaka Bursary is one of the best funding options in South Africa. It covers tuition, accommodation, books, and gives you a monthly living allowance.

In exchange, you agree to teach at a public school for the same number of years you received funding. Returning bursars must apply on the Funza Lushaka website by 30 November 2026, while brand new teaching students have until 31 January 2027.

3. Corporate and Postgraduate Bursaries (Closing Nov – Dec)

Several private companies and national research bodies keep their funding open through late summer. The National Research Foundation (NRF) closes its honours funding in late November, while private firms like PSG and Milpark accept applications well into December.

Many local municipalities also publish their mayoral bursaries between November and January once matric exams wrap up. Keep an eye on your local municipal website or visit your town hall to pick up physical forms.

What Documents Do You Need to Apply?

Do not wait until the closing day to look for your paperwork. Gather these certified copies right now:

  • Your South African green barcoded ID or smart ID card.
  • Certified ID copies of your parents or legal guardians.
  • Proof of household income (latest payslips, pension slips, or a SASSA letter).
  • An official affidavit if your parents are unemployed or single.
  • Your latest Grade 12 results or current university transcript.

When preparing your documents, following our checklist of proven bursary application steps will prevent simple errors that cause applications to get rejected.

Final Advice: Submit Even If Your Marks Aren't Perfect

Many students do not apply because they think their marks are too low. However, bursaries like NSFAS care primarily about household financial need rather than straight-A report cards.

Upload clear, readable scans, check your email daily for status updates, and never pay anyone money to submit a bursary application for you.

articles.title: High-Demand Degrees in South Africa: 2026 Career Guide
articles.content:
Choosing what to study at university is one of the most important decisions you will ever make. With South Africa’s youth unemployment rate sitting at challenging levels, picking a qualification that companies are actively hiring for gives you an immediate head start.

Every year, the Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET) publishes its National List of Occupations in High Demand (OIHD). This report tracks the exact career skills South African businesses, hospitals, banks, and public institutions desperately need.

If you are a high school matriculant, a current university student, or a parent planning tuition, this comprehensive guide highlights the high demand degrees in South Africa that offer strong job security, solid starting salaries, and long-term career growth.

Key Fact: According to Stats SA graduate surveys, university graduates in South Africa experience an unemployment rate of under 10%—far lower than the national average. Choosing an in-demand degree lowers that risk even further.

Why Your Choice of Degree Matters More Than Ever in 2026

Gone are the days when simply having any generic degree guaranteed a desk job after graduation. Employers today look for practical, technical, and analytical qualifications that solve immediate business problems.

Certain professions consistently face shortages of qualified graduates in South Africa. When supply is low and demand is high, employers compete for talent by offering higher starting salaries and quicker promotions.

To help fund your studies in these key fields, you should also check our guide on how to apply for bursaries in South Africa, as corporate bursary sponsors heavily favor in-demand degrees.

1. Computer Science and Software Engineering

South Africa’s digital economy is expanding rapidly across banking, insurance, retail, and telecommunications. Major local banks like Standard Bank, Capitec, and Discovery hire hundreds of software developers, cybersecurity analysts, and cloud architects each year.

A Bachelor of Science (BSc) in Computer Science or a Bachelor of Engineering (BEng) in Software Engineering prepares you to build enterprise systems, mobile applications, and secure networks.

Graduates entering this sector regularly earn starting salaries between R28,000 and R42,000 per month, with seasoned senior engineers reaching well into six figures. You can also explore our review of the 7 in-demand tech skills South African companies want.

  • Key Roles: Full-Stack Software Developer, Cloud Engineer, Cybersecurity Analyst.
  • Typical APS Requirement: 34 to 42 points (requires pure Mathematics Level 6 or higher).
  • Top Institutions: University of the Witwatersrand (Wits), University of Cape Town (UCT), University of Pretoria (UP), and Stellenbosch University.

2. Data Science and Business Analytics

Modern businesses generate massive streams of customer data, transaction records, and market metrics every second. Companies need skilled specialists who can turn raw data into profitable business decisions.

Degrees in Data Science, Statistics, and Mathematical Sciences are among the fastest-growing qualifications in the country. Because machine learning and artificial intelligence are revolutionizing local commerce, data talent is in massive demand.

Starting pay for junior data scientists and analysts typically ranges from R30,000 to R45,000 per month. If you want to see how these careers stack up against other fields, take a look at which degrees lead to the highest-paying jobs in South Africa.

  • Key Roles: Data Scientist, Business Intelligence Developer, Machine Learning Specialist.
  • Typical APS Requirement: 35 to 40 points.
  • Core Subjects: Pure Mathematics Level 6, Information Technology, or AP Maths.

3. Engineering: Civil, Electrical, and Renewable Energy

South Africa’s ongoing power grid upgrades, water treatment projects, and solar farm developments mean qualified engineers remain a fixture on the national scarce skills list.

Graduates with accredited qualifications recognized by the Engineering Council of South Africa (ECSA) find work across consulting firms, mining houses, state utilities, and independent power producers.

For an in-depth breakdown of engineering compensation packages, see our dedicated guide on the 10 highest paying engineering jobs in South Africa.

  • Key Specializations: Electrical Engineering, Renewable Energy, Civil Infrastructure, and Mechanical Engineering.
  • Typical APS Requirement: 36 to 42 points (requires Physical Sciences and Pure Mathematics at Level 6 or above).
  • Starting Pay: R27,000 to R40,000 per month depending on the industry.

4. Accounting and Financial Sciences (CA Track)

Chartered Accountants in South Africa, designated as CA(SA), remain among the most respected and employable professionals in the nation. The South African Institute of Chartered Accountants (SAICA) sets rigorous standards that are admired globally.

Students who complete a SAICA-accredited Bachelor of Accounting Science or BCom Accounting degree followed by their CTA (Certificate in the Theory of Accounting) rarely struggle to find employment.

Large audit firms (PwC, Deloitte, EY, KPMG) and multinational corporations absorb hundreds of trainee accountants into 3-year training contracts every single year.

  • Key Roles: Trainee Accountant, Financial Analyst, Internal Auditor, Tax Consultant.
  • Typical APS Requirement: 32 to 38 points (pure Mathematics Level 5 or 6 required; Mathematical Literacy is usually excluded).
  • Career Trajectory: Trainee salaries start around R18,000 to R26,000 per month during articles, jumping to R55,000+ per month immediately after qualification.

5. Healthcare, Medicine, and Pharmacy

The healthcare system in South Africa—both in state hospitals and the private sector—faces a permanent shortage of medical doctors, specialized nurses, and clinical pharmacists.

A Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBChB) guarantees immediate placement into mandatory paid two-year medical internship and one-year community service programmes with the Department of Health.

Pharmacy graduates (BPharm) and nursing science graduates also enjoy near-100% employment rates across retail pharmacies, public clinics, and private hospital groups.

  • Key Roles: Medical Doctor, Clinical Pharmacist, Registered Nurse, Sonographer.
  • Typical APS Requirement: 38 to 45 points (extremely competitive entry).
  • Starting Pay: Medical interns earn approximately R45,000 to R55,000 per month (inclusive of allowances).

6. Supply Chain and Logistics Management

South Africa is the economic gateway to Southern Africa, boasting major commercial ports in Durban, Cape Town, and Port Elizabeth, alongside massive freight corridors.

The rise of regional e-commerce, automated warehousing, and global trade challenges has elevated Supply Chain Management into one of the country's hottest commercial qualifications.

A BCom in Supply Chain Management or Logistics equips students to manage distribution networks, inventory, and cross-border customs operations.

  • Key Roles: Supply Chain Planner, Logistics Coordinator, Procurement Specialist.
  • Typical APS Requirement: 28 to 34 points.
  • Starting Pay: R20,000 to R32,000 per month.

7. STEM Education and High School Teaching

South Africa has an urgent, well-documented shortage of qualified high school educators who can teach Mathematics, Physical Sciences, and Technical subjects.

A Bachelor of Education (BEd) degree specializing in the Senior Phase and Further Education and Training (FET) phase provides guaranteed career openings, especially in growing secondary schools across both public and independent school sectors.

In addition, the Funza Lushaka Bursary programme fully funds tuition, accommodation, and allowances for eligible students who commit to teaching STEM subjects after graduating.

  • Key Roles: Mathematics Teacher, Physical Sciences Teacher, Coding & Robotics Educator.
  • Typical APS Requirement: 26 to 32 points.
  • Starting Pay: R22,000 to R28,000 per month on government entry scales (REQV 14).

Summary Table: Degrees, Starting Salaries, and APS Requirements

Here is how the top high-demand degrees in South Africa compare side-by-side on key metrics:

Degree Field Average Starting Pay Minimum APS Range Key High School Requirement
BSc Computer Science / IT R28,000 – R42,000 / month 34 – 42 Pure Maths Level 6 (70%+)
BSc / BEng Engineering R27,000 – R40,000 / month 36 – 42 Pure Maths & Physical Sciences Level 6
MBChB (Medicine & Surgery) R45,000 – R55,000 / month (Intern) 38 – 45+ Pure Maths, Physical & Life Sciences
BCom Accounting (CA Track) R18,000 – R26,000 (Articles) 32 – 38 Pure Maths Level 5 or 6 (60–70%)
BSc Data Science / Statistics R30,000 – R45,000 / month 35 – 40 Pure Maths Level 6 (70%+)
BCom Supply Chain Management R20,000 – R32,000 / month 28 – 34 Maths or Maths Lit Level 5
BEd (STEM Senior & FET Phase) R22,000 – R28,000 / month 26 – 32 Subject pass in Maths or Science

Key High School Subjects You Need to Protect

One of the biggest hurdles South African learners face when applying to university is subject choice. Many students drop pure Mathematics for Mathematical Literacy in Grade 10 without realizing they are disqualifying themselves from engineering, computer science, medicine, and accounting.

If you want to keep your doors open to high-demand careers, protecting your pure Mathematics mark is vital by mastering proven matric maths exam techniques.

You can verify current national workforce shortages directly on the Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET) portal and review the critical skills guidelines published on the official South African Government portal.

Step-by-Step Checklist for Picking Your Degree

  1. Calculate your realistic APS: Use your latest Grade 11 or Grade 12 results to see which faculties you realistically qualify for.
  2. Check the subject prerequisites: Never assume a university will admit you with Mathematical Literacy for a science or commerce degree.
  3. Review graduate hiring data: Confirm that the qualification appears on the DHET Occupations in High Demand list.
  4. Apply to at least 3 institutions: Apply early to a mix of traditional universities and universities of technology to protect yourself against faculty caps.
  5. Secure funding early: Submit your application via the official NSFAS portal and apply for private bursaries well before closing deadlines.

articles.title: How to Apply for Bursaries in South Africa: Legit Websites and Funding Guide
articles.content:
Paying for university in South Africa is not cheap. Tuition, registration, accommodation, food, transport, textbooks and other study costs can quickly become too much for one family to handle.

The good news is that there are many bursaries and funding opportunities available. The difficult part is finding the right ones, applying before the deadline and making sure you are using a legitimate website.

If you are a matric learner, university student or someone planning to study next year, this guide will show you where to look and how to apply.

What is a bursary?

A bursary is financial support given to a student to help pay for their education.

Depending on the bursary, it may cover some or all of your:

  • Tuition fees
  • Registration fees
  • Accommodation
  • Meals
  • Books and learning materials
  • Transport
  • Living expenses
  • Laptop or other study equipment

Not every bursary covers everything. Some only pay tuition, while others are much more comprehensive.

Some bursaries also come with conditions. For example, certain company bursaries may require you to work for the company after you graduate.

Always read the full terms and conditions before accepting funding.

Who can apply for a bursary?

There is no single rule for every bursary.

Different organisations may look at different things, including:

  • Your academic results
  • Your household income
  • Your field of study
  • Your year of study
  • Your age
  • Your province or municipality
  • Your university
  • Your nationality
  • Whether you come from a disadvantaged background
  • Whether your qualification is considered a scarce skill

Some bursaries are specifically for fields such as engineering, medicine, accounting, computer science, teaching, agriculture or law.

Others are available across several fields.

This is why you should not only apply for one bursary and wait for the answer. Apply for every legitimate opportunity where you meet the requirements.

Step 1: Know exactly what you are studying

Before searching for funding, write down your:

  • Qualification
  • University or college
  • Year of study
  • Expected graduation year
  • Average mark
  • Main subjects
  • Career field

For example, someone studying Computer Science should search for bursaries that specifically fund Computer Science, Information Technology, Data Science, Engineering or other related fields.

The more specific your search is, the easier it becomes to find bursaries that actually match you.

Step 2: Start with NSFAS

If you are studying at a public university or TVET college and meet the financial and other requirements, check the National Student Financial Aid Scheme first.

NSFAS is the main government funding scheme for students who cannot afford tertiary education. Its bursary funding can cover things such as registration, tuition, learning materials and certain allowances, depending on the applicable rules.

Applications are made through the official NSFAS website and myNSFAS account.

Do not apply through someone claiming they can "guarantee" NSFAS funding for you.

Official NSFAS website: www.nsfas.org.za

NSFAS says applicants should create a myNSFAS profile, complete the required information and submit their application online. (NSFAS)

Step 3: Check your university's financial aid office

A lot of students make the mistake of searching only on Google.

Your university itself can be one of the best places to find funding.

Universities may offer:

  • University bursaries
  • Merit awards
  • Financial aid
  • Faculty-specific funding
  • Scholarships
  • Donor-funded bursaries
  • Emergency financial assistance
  • Residence-related funding

The South African government also recommends that students check with their university's financial aid office for bursaries and awards. (Department of Basic Education)

Go to your university's official website and search for:

  • Financial Aid
  • or
  • Student Funding
  • or
  • Bursaries

Do not rely on a random Facebook post when your university has published the information officially.

Step 4: Look at government bursaries

South African government departments offer bursaries for different fields.

Some are aimed at specific careers and skills that government needs.

One example is the Funza Lushaka Bursary, which supports students studying towards teaching qualifications in priority subject areas.

Funza Lushaka is applied for through the official government e-Services system. The programme also has specific requirements and a service obligation after graduation. (Funza Lushaka)

Official Funza Lushaka website: www.funzalushaka.doe.gov.za

You should also check government departments, provincial governments and municipalities for bursaries.

Some municipal bursaries are restricted to students who live in that municipality.

Step 5: Check companies and organisations

Many South African companies offer bursaries because they need skilled graduates in specific industries.

Examples include:

  • Eskom
  • Transnet
  • Vodacom
  • CSIR
  • Sasol Foundation
  • SANRAL
  • Standard Bank
  • SAICA
  • Various SETAs
  • Banks and financial institutions
  • Mining companies
  • Engineering companies
  • Insurance companies
  • Technology companies

For example, Eskom awarded 200 bursaries for the 2026 financial year, while Transnet offers full-time bursaries in areas including Computer Science, Cyber Security, Data Analytics, engineering and other fields. (Eskom)

The CSIR also offers bursaries for undergraduate and postgraduate students in priority science, engineering and technology fields. (CSIR)

The important part is this:

Apply on the organisation's official website whenever possible.

Do not automatically trust a website just because it has the company's logo on it.

Legitimate bursary websites to bookmark

To help you choose the right bursary scheme, here is a breakdown of major South African funding programs, eligibility rules, and what each package covers:

Bursary Scheme Target Fields Eligibility Criteria Coverage & Benefits Official Portal
NSFAS All undergraduate degrees & TVET diplomas Combined household income ≤ R350,000 / year (or SASSA recipient) 100% Tuition, accommodation, meals, book & personal allowance nsfas.org.za
Funza Lushaka Bachelor of Education (BEd) & PGCE in priority subjects South African citizen, 30+ APS or teaching priority subject pass Full tuition, accommodation, living allowances & guaranteed placement funzalushaka.doe.gov.za
Thuthuka Bursary (SAICA) BCom Accounting (Chartered Accountant track) Black/Coloured SA citizen, Level 5 (60%+) in pure Mathematics Full tuition, accommodation, books, academic coaching & mentorship saica.org.za
Sasol Bursary Programme Engineering, Chemistry, Data Science, Metallurgy Level 6 (70%+) in Maths & Physical Science; SA citizen Tuition, accommodation, meal allowance, laptop, holiday work placement sasolbursaries.com
SETA Bursaries (CHIETA, MERSETA) Artisans, Technical trades, STEM degrees Unemployed youth, meets university/college minimum admission criteria Tuition, learning material allowance, practical trade training funding dhet.gov.za

Here are websites worth keeping on your list.

Official government and funding websites

NSFAS
www.nsfas.org.za
For government-funded tertiary education support at public universities and TVET colleges.

Funza Lushaka
www.funzalushaka.doe.gov.za
For eligible students pursuing teaching qualifications.

South African Government
www.gov.za
Useful for government information and finding official funding information.

Department of Higher Education and Training
www.dhet.gov.za
Useful for higher education information and government programmes.

Official company and organisation websites

Eskom
www.eskom.co.za
Check Eskom's official website for bursary and youth development opportunities. Eskom has an established bursary programme supporting students in fields linked to its skills requirements. (Eskom)

Transnet
www.transnet.net
Transnet offers undergraduate bursaries across technical and non-technical fields. (Transnet)

CSIR
www.csir.co.za
A particularly useful website for students interested in science, technology, engineering, Computer Science, IT and related fields. (CSIR)

SAICA Thuthuka
www.saica.org.za
Useful for students pursuing the CA(SA) route through eligible BCom Accounting programmes. (SAICA)

Vodacom
www.vodacom.com
Vodacom has an external bursary programme for qualifying students, particularly in STEM-related fields. (Vodacom)

Bursary listing websites

You can also use bursary directories to discover opportunities.

Careers Portal
www.careersportal.co.za
Careers Portal publishes bursary opportunities and application deadlines. (Careers Portal)

Bursaries Portal
www.bursariesportal.co.za
Another useful directory that lists bursaries from companies, government organisations and other institutions. (Bursaries Portal)

These websites are useful for finding opportunities, but you should still check the original organisation's website before submitting personal information.

Official website or bursary directory?

This distinction matters.

A bursary directory can tell you:
"Company X is offering a bursary."
But the company's own website should be your final check.

For example:
Bursary directory → Find the opportunity → Open the organisation's official website → Check requirements → Apply through the official application system.

That is much safer than clicking the first "Apply Now" button you see on Google.

Documents you should prepare

Do not wait until the day before the deadline to start looking for documents.

Create a folder on your computer called:
Bursary Applications 2027
Keep copies of commonly requested documents inside it.

These can include:

  • South African ID
  • Matric certificate
  • Latest academic results
  • Full academic transcript
  • Proof of registration
  • Proof of university acceptance
  • Proof of application
  • Proof of household income
  • Parents' or guardians' income documents where required
  • Affidavits where applicable
  • Proof of residence
  • Updated CV
  • Motivational letter
  • Other documents specifically requested by the bursary

Different bursaries require different documents, so do not upload random documents just because another bursary asked for them.

For example, CSIR's bursary requirements include an updated CV, certified ID and latest academic record for its relevant applications. (CSIR)

Make your motivational letter count

Some bursaries ask for a motivational letter.

Do not write:
"I need this bursary because my family is poor and I want to study."

Explain your situation properly.

A good motivation should answer:

  • Who are you?
  • What are you studying?
  • Why did you choose the qualification?
  • What have you achieved academically?
  • Why do you need financial assistance?
  • What are your career goals?
  • Why are you suitable for the bursary?
  • What do you want to contribute after graduating?

Keep it honest.

Do not copy someone else's motivational letter from TikTok or Google and change the name.

Apply early

This is one of the biggest mistakes students make.

A bursary can close before you even hear about it.

Some programmes have deadlines many months before the new academic year begins.

For example, CSIR's 2027 bursary applications closed on 15 September 2026. (CSIR)

Other 2027 bursaries are still being advertised around September 2026, showing why students should check regularly rather than searching only once. (Careers Portal)

If you find a bursary that matches you, apply immediately.

Do not wait until the closing date.

Apply for multiple bursaries

There is no rule saying you must apply for only one bursary.

Apply for several opportunities that you genuinely qualify for.

For example:

  • NSFAS
  • University funding
  • Government bursaries
  • Company bursaries
  • SETA bursaries
  • Municipal or provincial bursaries
  • Field-specific bursaries
  • Scholarships

Just remember that some funding programmes have rules about receiving other funding at the same time.

Always disclose existing funding when an application asks for it.

Be careful of bursary scams

This is where you need to be very careful.

A bursary application should not require you to send your banking password, banking PIN or OTP to a random person.

Be suspicious if someone says:

  • "Pay R200 and we will guarantee your bursary."
  • "Send me your OTP so I can complete your application."
  • "Send your banking password."
  • "You have won a bursary you never applied for."
  • "We guarantee funding."
  • "Pay us and we will make NSFAS approve you."

Those are major red flags.

Use official websites and verify the organisation before submitting sensitive information.

Government departments and companies also warn the public about scams involving requests for sensitive information. (South African Revenue Service)

How to keep track of applications

Make a simple spreadsheet.

Use columns like:

  • Bursary
  • Organisation
  • Website
  • Closing date
  • Requirements
  • Applied?
  • Result

This makes a massive difference when you are applying for many opportunities.

The easiest bursary strategy

If you are serious about getting funding, use this routine:

Every week:

  • Check NSFAS.
  • Check your university's funding page.
  • Check government bursaries.
  • Check Careers Portal.
  • Check Bursaries Portal.
  • Check companies in your industry.
  • Search for bursaries using your exact degree.
  • Check closing dates.
  • Apply immediately when you qualify.
  • Save proof that you submitted the application.

For example, instead of searching only:
"bursaries South Africa"
search:
"Computer Science bursaries South Africa"
"Accounting bursaries South Africa"
"Engineering bursaries South Africa"
"Nursing bursaries South Africa"
"Bursaries for current university students"
"Bursaries for second year students"

Your field of study can lead you to opportunities that a general search will miss.

Final tip: don't give up after one rejection

Getting rejected for one bursary does not mean you cannot get funding somewhere else.

Bursaries have different requirements, budgets, fields of study and selection processes.

Keep applying.

The goal is not to find one magical bursary website.

The goal is to build a list of legitimate funding opportunities, check them regularly and apply to the ones that match your situation.

And before you submit anything, ask yourself one question:
"Am I applying through the real organisation, or am I giving my personal information to a random website?"

If you are not sure, stop and verify the website first.

articles.title: How to Pass Your Driving Test in South Africa: K53 Tips That Actually Help
articles.content:
The best way to pass your South African driving test is to practise the K53 procedures correctly, master the yard manoeuvres, practise observation and road positioning, and get comfortable driving in real traffic. Don't just practise driving around. Practise the specific skills you will be assessed on.

Getting your driver's licence in South Africa can feel stressful.

You practise for weeks. You spend money on driving lessons. You learn the K53 system. Then the test day arrives and suddenly you forget everything you thought you knew.

But passing your driving licence test is not about being a perfect driver. It is about being prepared, calm and consistent.

What You Need to Know About the South African Driving Test

The South African practical driving test is based on the K53 system and includes a yard test and a road test. The test is designed to assess your ability to handle the vehicle, follow traffic rules and deal with real traffic situations.

The official K53 practical driving test documentation describes the test as consisting of a yard test and a road test, assessing vehicle handling, obedience to traffic rules and the ability to cope with traffic situations.

So, how do you actually give yourself the best chance of passing? Let's break it down.

How to Prepare for Your K53 Driving Test

Before you start practising, understand what the test involves. For a normal light motor vehicle, the practical test has two main parts: the yard test and the road test.

Learn the K53 system

One of the biggest mistakes learners make is treating K53 like a list of movements they need to memorise. K53 is more than that. You need to understand the procedures and develop the habit of doing them correctly.

For example, when changing lanes, you should not simply look in your mirror and move over. You need to follow the correct observation and signalling procedure. The same applies to intersections, stopping, turning, moving off and other situations. The goal is to make these actions automatic.

Practise the yard test

Do not wait until the week of your test to start practising the yard manoeuvres. Practise them repeatedly. The goal is not to rush. Slow and controlled is better than fast and messy.

Practise driving on real roads

Knowing one familiar road does not mean you are ready for the test. Try driving in different environments such as quiet residential streets, busy roads, intersections, traffic circles, and roads with pedestrians.

Work on your weak points

If you make the same mistake during every lesson, don't just keep driving and hope it disappears. Stop and fix it. If you struggle with clutch control, spend more time practising moving off smoothly. Your lessons should target your weaknesses.

K53 Yard Test Tips

The yard test checks things such as vehicle control and specific manoeuvres. Depending on your test and vehicle, this can include:

  • Pre-trip vehicle inspection
  • Starting procedures
  • Incline start (hill start)
  • Alley docking
  • Parallel parking
  • Turning in the road
  • Stopping procedures

Your instructor should teach you the exact procedure required for your test. Practise until you can perform each manoeuvre without panicking.

K53 Road Test Tips

The road test checks how you drive in actual traffic and whether you follow the required procedures and rules. This is one of the most important parts of driving. Do not only focus on where the car is going. You need to constantly be aware of what is happening around you.

Practise checking:

  • Your mirrors
  • Blind spots
  • Indicating correctly before manoeuvres
  • Intersections and traffic circles
  • Lane changes
  • Following distances and stopping

You should eventually be checking your surroundings naturally rather than only doing it because you remembered that the examiner is watching.

Common Mistakes That Can Make You Fail

Here is a breakdown of critical K53 driving test faults, penalty point consequences, and how to avoid an instant fail:

K53 Test Stage Critical Action / Manoeuvre Penalty Type Examiner's Rule
Incline Start (Hill Start) Moving off smoothly on a steep incline Instant Disqualification if vehicle rolls back > 15cm Keep handbrake firmly up until engine reaches clutch friction point; release smoothly without revving excessively.
Alley Docking & Parallel Parking Reverse parking between boundary poles within 3 movements Instant Disqualification for touching any pole or mounting kerb Perform 360-degree blind spot observation before moving; steer deliberately at idle speed.
Traffic Intersections & Stop Signs Full vehicle stop behind the white demarcation line Instant Disqualification for rolling stop or crossing red light Count a full 3-second standstill; check rear mirror and blind spots left and right before proceeding.
Lane Changing & Turning Mirror-Indicator-Blindspot Sequence (M-I-B) Demerit Points (accumulation leads to test failure) Check center and side mirror, signal for at least 30 meters, perform head-turn blind spot check, then steer smoothly.
Emergency Stop Test Rapid controlled braking without skidding or stalling Demerit Points for uncontrolled skid or hands slipping off wheel Brake hard and progressively with both hands firmly at 10-to-2 on steering wheel; depress clutch just before stopping.

If you remember nothing else from this article, remember these common mistakes to avoid:

  • Do not rush. Accelerating too quickly or rushing manoeuvres is a fast track to failing.
  • Do not ignore observations. Failing to check mirrors and blind spots correctly is a major issue.
  • Rolling stops. Always come to a complete stop at stop signs.
  • Incorrect positioning and hitting kerbs. Especially during yard manoeuvres.
  • Do not forget your procedures.
  • Do not drive differently just because the examiner is sitting next to you.

The exact scoring and immediate-failure rules are based on the prescribed K53 testing procedure, so make sure your instructor is teaching you the current requirements for your vehicle class and testing centre.

How to Stay Calm During Your Driving Test

Your examiner is sitting next to you. Your heart is beating. You suddenly forget everything you've practised. This is where many learners get themselves into trouble. They become nervous and start driving differently from how they normally drive.

Take your time. Listen carefully to the examiner's instructions. If you do not hear or understand an instruction, make sure you understand what you are being asked to do before proceeding.

If you make a small mistake, don't panic. Making one mistake does not automatically mean you have failed. If you make a mistake, stay calm and continue driving safely. Do not let one mistake cause another five mistakes.

What to Do the Day Before Your Driving Test

The day before your test should not be an eight-hour driving marathon. You want to be confident, not exhausted.

Have a focused practice session. Go through the things you normally struggle with. Review your K53 procedures. Make sure you know where you need to go for your test. Then get some rest. Being tired and stressed on test day will not help you.

Make sure you have the documents you need. According to the South African Government, you need your learner's licence, ID, required photographs, proof of residential address and booking fee when applying for a driving licence. You should also keep your booking receipt because it confirms your test date and time. Requirements can vary slightly by testing centre, so check with your DLTC beforehand.

What to Do on the Morning of Your Test

Keep things simple. Eat something if you normally eat breakfast. Drink some water. Give yourself enough time to get there. The government states that you must arrive at the DLTC at the specified testing time, where your documents will be checked before you proceed with the test.

Do not spend the entire morning watching scary TikTok videos about people failing their driving tests. Trust your preparation.

What Happens If You Fail Your Driving Test?

There is nothing embarrassing about needing more practice. If you do fail, use it as a learning opportunity. Ask your examiner where you went wrong, take extra lessons, and work specifically on those weaknesses before booking your next test.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you fail your driving test for stalling?

Stalling once does not necessarily mean an immediate failure, depending on where and how it happens. However, repeatedly stalling or stalling in a dangerous position (like an intersection) will cause you to lose points or fail. The key is to restart the car calmly and safely.

What are the most common K53 mistakes?

Some of the most common mistakes include failing to check blind spots, rolling through stop signs, hitting the kerb during parking manoeuvres, rolling backwards on an incline start, and not using the parking brake correctly.

What should I take to my driving test?

You generally need your valid learner's licence, your South African ID, the booking receipt, and the required fees for issuing the licence if you pass. Check with your specific DLTC for any additional requirements like photographs or proof of address.

What happens during the K53 yard test?

The yard test happens in a controlled area at the testing centre. You will perform a pre-trip inspection, and complete manoeuvres like alley docking, parallel parking, a three-point turn, and an incline start without hitting obstacles or rolling.

What happens during the K53 road test?

During the road test, the examiner will direct you along a route in normal traffic. You will be assessed on how you observe the road, use your mirrors, signal, change lanes, approach intersections, and obey traffic signs and speed limits.

articles.title: Which Degrees Lead to the Highest-Paying Jobs in South Africa? 2026 Guide
articles.content:
Let’s be honest.

When you are choosing a degree, one of the questions that eventually comes up is:

“Will I actually make good money with this degree?”

It is a fair question.

South Africa has a tough job market. In the second quarter of 2026, the official unemployment rate was 33.6%, with about 8.5 million people unemployed. Youth unemployment was even higher, at 47.4%. (Statistics South Africa)

So choosing a degree is not just about studying something you like. You also want to understand where that degree can take you, what careers it can lead to and which industries have strong earning potential.

But there is something important to understand first.

A degree does not guarantee a high salary.

Your experience, skills, industry, location and level of responsibility can make a huge difference.

So, which degrees can lead to some of the highest-paying careers in South Africa?

Let’s look at them.

1. Computer Science

Computer Science is one of the most flexible degrees you can choose if you are interested in technology.

You are not limited to becoming a programmer.

A Computer Science graduate can move into areas such as:

  • Software engineering
  • Data science
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Machine learning
  • Cybersecurity
  • Cloud computing
  • Data engineering
  • Systems analysis
  • Technology consulting

South Africa's National List of Occupations in High Demand includes occupations such as ICT Systems Analyst and Data Scientist, while software development and related ICT occupations have also been identified in national skills planning. (South Africa Government)

The current job market also shows demand for software engineers and data professionals. Pnet currently lists thousands of software engineering and data science opportunities in South Africa, although job-board counts change constantly. (Pnet)

The earning potential becomes particularly interesting when you move into specialised areas such as AI, machine learning, cloud architecture, cybersecurity or senior software engineering.

For example, a current Pnet listing for a senior machine learning engineer in Sandton advertises R100,000 to R130,000 per month. That is a senior-level example, not a graduate salary, but it shows the earning potential that specialised technical skills can reach. (Pnet)

Bottom line: If you enjoy technology, mathematics and problem-solving, Computer Science can open doors to some of the highest-paying careers in the technology industry.

2. Mathematics

You might not immediately think of Mathematics as a high-paying degree.

But mathematics is extremely useful in industries where companies need people who can analyse data, build models and solve complicated problems.

A Mathematics graduate can move into areas such as:

  • Data science
  • Statistics
  • Actuarial work
  • Quantitative finance
  • Financial modelling
  • Machine learning
  • Risk analysis
  • Research
  • Technology

Modern data science jobs show just how connected these fields have become. Current Pnet listings for data scientists accept degrees in Mathematics, Statistics, Computer Science, Engineering, Data Science and other quantitative fields. (Pnet)

Mathematics can therefore be particularly valuable when combined with programming, statistics, finance or computer science.

Bottom line: Mathematics can be a powerful degree if you build practical skills around it.

3. Statistics and Data Science

Data is becoming increasingly important to businesses.

Companies collect huge amounts of information, but that information is not very useful unless someone can analyse it and turn it into something meaningful.

That is where data professionals come in.

Career options include:

  • Data Scientist
  • Data Analyst
  • Machine Learning Engineer
  • Business Intelligence Analyst
  • Quantitative Analyst
  • Data Engineer
  • Risk Analyst

Current Pnet vacancies show employers looking for data scientists with backgrounds in areas including Computer Science, Mathematics, Statistics, Engineering and Data Science. (Pnet)

The National List of Occupations in High Demand also includes Data Scientist. (South Africa Government)

The combination of statistics, programming and business knowledge can therefore be extremely valuable.

Bottom line: If you enjoy numbers and analysing problems, Statistics or Data Science can lead to strong career opportunities.

4. Engineering

Engineering remains one of the strongest professional fields because engineers solve real-world problems across industries.

Depending on your specialisation, you could work in:

  • Mining
  • Manufacturing
  • Energy
  • Construction
  • Automotive
  • Telecommunications
  • Technology
  • Infrastructure
  • Robotics
  • Automation

Engineering can also overlap heavily with technology.

For example, software, robotics, artificial intelligence and automation are increasingly connected to traditional engineering fields.

The Council on Higher Education recognises engineering as one of South Africa's major higher-education fields, alongside areas such as Computer and Information Sciences, Business, Health, Law and Mathematics and Statistics. (CHE)

Bottom line: Engineering can offer strong earning potential, especially when you specialise and gain experience.

5. Finance

Finance is another field where specialised skills can lead to high-paying careers.

A finance-related qualification can lead to roles such as:

  • Financial Analyst
  • Investment Analyst
  • Risk Analyst
  • Financial Manager
  • Investment Manager
  • Financial Advisor
  • Financial Modelling Analyst
  • Quantitative Finance roles

SAQA qualification information shows that finance and accounting qualifications can lead to careers across accounting, finance, management, financial advising, auditing, taxation and financial analysis. (SAQA)

Finance also plays a major role in South Africa's economy. Stats SA's employment statistics track business services as a major employment and earnings category, while finance was one of the industries that recorded employment growth in Q2 2026. (Statistics South Africa)

Bottom line: Finance can be particularly rewarding if you move into specialised areas such as investments, risk, financial modelling or management.

6. Accounting

Accounting may not sound exciting to everyone, but it can lead to some very strong professional careers.

Possible careers include:

  • Accountant
  • Chartered Accountant
  • Auditor
  • Tax Specialist
  • Financial Manager
  • Management Accountant
  • Internal Auditor
  • Financial Analyst

SAQA states that accounting qualifications can prepare learners for careers in accounting, auditing, taxation, management accounting and finance. Some qualifications specifically form part of the pathway towards becoming a Chartered Accountant. (SAQA)

The important thing here is professional progression.

Someone starting in an entry-level accounting position is obviously not going to earn the same amount as an experienced professional in a senior financial role.

Bottom line: Accounting can provide a structured career path, especially for people who continue with professional qualifications and gain experience.

7. Law

Law is another degree with a wide range of career possibilities.

You could work in:

  • Corporate law
  • Commercial law
  • Tax law
  • Labour law
  • Litigation
  • Banking and finance
  • Compliance
  • Legal consulting
  • Government

Law can also overlap with business.

For example, companies need legal professionals who understand contracts, regulations, corporate structures and commercial risks.

The South African higher-education system recognises Law as a distinct field of study, with areas including company law, criminal law, human rights, private law and public law. (CHE)

However, law is another field where your eventual earnings depend heavily on your specialisation, experience and the type of organisation you work for.

Bottom line: Law can be highly rewarding, particularly when combined with valuable commercial or specialist knowledge.

8. Economics

Economics gives you a strong foundation for understanding markets, businesses, government policy and financial systems.

Career paths can include:

  • Economist
  • Economic Analyst
  • Financial Analyst
  • Policy Analyst
  • Researcher
  • Consultant
  • Data Analyst
  • Investment-related roles

Economics can also work very well when combined with mathematics, statistics, finance or programming.

For example, someone who combines economics with strong quantitative and programming skills can move into areas such as financial modelling, data analysis and quantitative finance.

Bottom line: Economics can become much more valuable when you add practical technical skills to the degree.

9. Electrical Engineering

Electrical Engineering deserves its own mention because of how broad the field is.

Electrical engineers can work in areas such as:

  • Energy
  • Telecommunications
  • Electronics
  • Automation
  • Control systems
  • Manufacturing
  • Robotics
  • Embedded systems
  • Renewable energy

The field can also overlap with software and computer engineering.

This means someone with electrical engineering skills can potentially work on both physical systems and modern technology.

South Africa's higher-education framework recognises engineering as a major field of study, while national skills planning continues to identify technical occupations as important to the economy. (CHE)

Bottom line: Electrical Engineering can offer strong opportunities, especially for people who specialise in areas connected to technology, energy or automation.

10. Logistics and Supply Chain

South Africa depends heavily on the movement of goods.

That makes logistics and supply chain an important part of the economy.

Possible careers include:

  • Supply Chain Manager
  • Logistics Manager
  • Procurement Specialist
  • Operations Manager
  • Transport Manager
  • Warehouse Manager
  • Supply Chain Analyst

The field combines business, operations, data and management.

As you gain experience and move into management or specialised positions, your earning potential can increase significantly.

Bottom line: Logistics may not get as much attention as technology or finance, but it can provide strong career opportunities.

11. Medicine and Health Sciences

Healthcare is another field where specialised qualifications can lead to strong careers.

Depending on the qualification, careers can include:

  • Doctor
  • Specialist physician
  • Surgeon
  • Pharmacist
  • Physiotherapist
  • Occupational therapist
  • Radiographer
  • Medical scientist
  • Other healthcare professionals

The health professions are recognised as a major field within South Africa's higher-education system. (CHE)

However, there is an important difference between saying a degree can lead to a high-paying career and saying that everyone with that degree will earn a high salary.

Healthcare careers often require additional professional training, registration and years of experience.

Bottom line: Medicine and specialised healthcare careers can have high earning potential, but they also require significant training and commitment.

12. Information Technology

Information Technology is another broad field.

An IT graduate can work in areas such as:

  • Systems administration
  • Networking
  • Cloud computing
  • Cybersecurity
  • IT support
  • Database administration
  • Business analysis
  • IT management
  • Software development

South Africa's national occupations-in-demand list includes ICT-related occupations such as ICT Systems Analyst and Data Scientist. (South Africa Government)

The current Pnet market also shows substantial activity in IT-related roles, including software engineering and data science. (Pnet)

Bottom line: IT can be a strong choice, but your specific skills matter. Someone with advanced cloud, cybersecurity or software skills may have very different earning potential from someone working in basic IT support.

13. Business Management

Business Management is one of the broadest degrees on this list.

It can lead to careers in:

  • Management
  • Sales
  • Marketing
  • Operations
  • Consulting
  • Business development
  • Human resources
  • Entrepreneurship

The Council on Higher Education lists Business, Economics and Management Studies as one of South Africa's major higher-education fields. (CHE)

The problem is that the degree itself does not automatically put you into a high-paying management position.

Usually, management positions come after you have developed experience and demonstrated that you can actually manage people, money, projects or operations.

Bottom line: Business degrees can become much more valuable when combined with industry experience and a specialised skill.

14. Psychology

Psychology is another popular degree, but it is important to understand the difference between having a psychology degree and becoming a practising psychologist.

A psychology qualification can open doors into areas such as:

  • Human resources
  • Research
  • Counselling-related fields
  • Organisational environments
  • Social services
  • Further professional training

Psychology is recognised as its own field of higher education in South Africa. (CHE)

If your goal is to become a registered psychologist, however, additional education, professional training and registration requirements apply.

Bottom line: Psychology can lead to meaningful careers, but it is not a degree where you should expect a high salary immediately after graduation.

15. Education

Education may not normally appear on lists of the country's highest-paying careers, but it remains an important professional field.

Career options can include:

  • Teacher
  • School management
  • Education administration
  • Curriculum development
  • Educational technology
  • Academic research
  • Education policy

Education is recognised as a major field in South Africa's higher-education system. (CHE)

Your earning potential will depend heavily on your qualification level, experience, role and employer.

Bottom line: Education is more about long-term professional development than becoming wealthy quickly.

What About Artificial Intelligence?

Artificial Intelligence deserves a special mention because it cuts across several degrees.

You do not necessarily need a degree called "Artificial Intelligence" to work in AI.

People entering AI-related careers can come from backgrounds such as:

  • Computer Science
  • Mathematics
  • Statistics
  • Data Science
  • Engineering
  • Actuarial Science

Current South African job listings demonstrate this overlap. Pnet vacancies for data science and machine learning roles commonly accept candidates from Computer Science, Mathematics, Statistics, Engineering and other quantitative disciplines. (Pnet)

South Africa's national occupations-in-demand information also identifies data and ICT-related occupations. (South Africa Government)

This is why AI can be an attractive specialisation.

You can take a traditional degree and then build additional skills in:

  • Python
  • Statistics
  • Machine learning
  • Data engineering
  • Cloud computing
  • Deep learning
  • AI systems
  • Software engineering

That combination can make you much more competitive.

So Which Degrees Are the Best?

Here is an at-a-glance comparison of the highest-paying degree pathways in South Africa, based on verified industry benchmarks and graduate earnings data:

Degree Pathway High-Paying Roles Typical Starting Pay Senior / Specialized Range
BSc Computer Science / IT Cloud Architect, AI Engineer, Full-Stack Dev R25,000 – R38,000 / month R900,000 – R1.8M / year
BEng / BSc Engineering Electrical Engineer, Mining Specialist, Project Lead R28,000 – R42,000 / month R950,000 – R2.0M / year
BSc Data Science & Maths Quantitative Analyst, Machine Learning Scientist R30,000 – R45,000 / month R1.1M – R2.2M / year
BCom Actuarial Science Actuarial Analyst, Risk Specialist, Chief Actuary R35,000 – R50,000 / month R1.3M – R2.5M+ / year
MBChB (Medicine & Health) Medical Doctor, Surgeon, Specialized Consultant R40,000 – R55,000 / month (Intern/ComServe) R1.2M – R3.0M+ / year
BCom Accounting (CA track) Chartered Accountant (CA(SA)), Financial Director R22,000 – R32,000 / month (Articles) R850,000 – R2.0M / year (Post-CA)
LLB (Law) Corporate Attorney, Commercial Advocate, Legal Advisor R18,000 – R30,000 / month (Candidate Attorney) R800,000 – R2.1M / year

There is no single answer.

If your main goal is earning potential, fields such as:

  • Computer Science
  • Mathematics
  • Data Science
  • Engineering
  • Finance
  • Accounting
  • Medicine
  • Law

can provide pathways into well-paid careers.

But the degree is only the beginning.

Two people can have the same degree and end up earning completely different salaries.

One might graduate, stop learning and struggle to find work.

The other might graduate with internships, projects, professional qualifications, technical skills and several years of experience.

Their careers can look completely different.

Your Skills Matter More Than You Think

This is probably the most important part.

Don't choose a degree only because someone told you it makes money.

Look at the skills the industry actually needs.

For example, current technology vacancies frequently ask for skills such as programming, SQL, cloud technologies, machine learning, data engineering and software development. (Pnet)

The same principle applies outside technology.

Finance needs people who understand financial analysis.

Engineering needs people who can solve technical problems.

Accounting needs people who understand financial reporting, taxation and auditing.

Law needs people who understand legal systems and can apply them to real problems.

The degree gives you the foundation.

Your skills make you useful.

One More Thing: South Africa's Job Market Is Tough

It is important not to ignore reality.

South Africa's official unemployment rate was 33.6% in Q2 2026. Youth unemployment was 47.4%. (Statistics South Africa)

That means getting a degree does not automatically mean you will walk into a high-paying job.

However, education can still make a difference.

In Q1 2026, Stats SA reported a graduate unemployment rate of 12.2%, substantially below the unemployment rates recorded for people with lower levels of education. (Statistics South Africa)

So the message is not:

“Get a degree and you will become rich.”

The message is:

“Get useful education, develop valuable skills and build experience.”

That combination gives you a much stronger position in the job market.

Final Word

South Africa's job market is difficult.

There are no guarantees.

But there are still industries where strong skills, experience and specialised knowledge can lead to excellent careers.

So choose carefully.

Build useful skills.

Get experience wherever you can.

And don't stop learning after you graduate.

Because the degree may get you through the door.

What you can actually do is what can keep you there.

  • Pnet Job Market Trends Reports: Used for current hiring and employment-market trends in South Africa. Pnet provides 2026 reports, including January, February, March, April and June reports. Pnet Job Market Trends Reports

Here are a few ideas.

Here is a quick comparison of the top bakkie side hustles in South Africa, what gear you will need, and realistic earning potential per trip or month:

Side Hustle Best Bakkie Type Essential Equipment Estimated Earning Potential
Furniture Moving & Student Relocation Single or Double Cab (Canopy or Open Bed) Heavy-duty tie-down straps, moving blankets, trolley R600 – R1,500 per local trip
Building Materials Delivery Single Cab (Dropside or 1-Tonne) Heavy tarpaulin cover, ratchet tie-downs, shovel R500 – R1,200 per hardware delivery
Garden Refuse & Rubble Removal Single Cab with high cattle rails / mesh Pitchfork, rakes, heavy-duty disposal bags, dump fee slip R450 – R900 per load
Mobile Spaza / Fresh Produce Supply Double Cab or Half-Tonne (e.g. NP200) Plastic crates, digital hanging scale, card machine R3,500 – R8,000 profit weekly
Weekend Bakkie Rental / Courier Contractor 1-Tonne Diesel Bakkie (Hilux, Isuzu, Ranger) GPS tracker, verified driver contract, roadside assist R800 – R1,400 daily hire fee

Move Furniture

You can help people move furniture when they move houses. Students are another good market, especially when they move between university residences, res and home.

Deliver Building Materials

People buy sand, bricks, cement and other building materials but don't always have a vehicle to transport them. You can work with local hardware stores or take direct orders from customers.

Start a Landscaping Business

Get a lawnmower, brush cutter and some basic gardening tools, then start offering garden maintenance in nearby suburbs. You can also approach schools, churches, businesses and other organisations that need their yards maintained.

Deliver Water

In areas that often experience water shortages, water delivery can become a useful service. If you have access to a legal and reliable water supply, you can deliver water to households and charge for the service.

Sell Fresh Produce

You can buy vegetables and fruit from farms or wholesalers and sell them in your community. A bakkie makes it easier to transport larger quantities and reach customers in different areas.

Rent Out Sound Equipment

If you have speakers, microphones and other sound equipment, you can offer them for birthdays, weddings, parties and community events. Your bakkie can also be used to transport and set up the equipment.

Transport Farm Produce

You can work with farmers who need their produce taken to markets, shops or customers. This can work particularly well in areas where farming is common.

Remove Garden Waste

People regularly cut grass, trees and bushes but don't always have a way to get rid of the waste. You can offer a collection service and charge per load or job.

Transport Equipment

Businesses and individuals often need equipment moved from one place to another. This could include tools, machinery, event equipment or stock. You can charge based on the distance and size of the job.

Find a Problem in Your Area

The best idea might not be on this list.

Look around your neighbourhood and see what people are struggling to get or what they are already paying others to do.

If there is a problem, and your bakkie can help solve it, you may have a business.

Don't just ask what you can do with a bakkie. Ask what your community needs and how your bakkie can provide it.

articles.title: Why Your Phone Knows So Much About You
articles.content:
Think about your phone for a second. Have you ever wondered exactly how your phone tracks you?

It knows where you go. It knows who you talk to. It knows what you search for, what videos you watch, what apps you use and, in some cases, what you are interested in buying.

And somehow, after searching for something once, you might suddenly start seeing adverts for it everywhere.

It can feel like your phone is reading your mind. It isn't. But the amount of information your phone and the apps on it can collect is pretty crazy.

How Does Your Phone Know Where You Are?

One of the main ways how your phone tracks you is by working out your location using GPS, Wi-Fi networks, Bluetooth and nearby cellphone towers.

This is useful when you open Google Maps and need directions. It is also useful when an app needs to show you something nearby. But location data can reveal much more than just a dot on a map.

If your phone regularly sees you at the same place every morning and another place every afternoon, it can help build a picture of your daily routine. Your location can show places you visit, how often you visit them and how long you normally stay there.

That is a lot of information from something as simple as your phone knowing where you are.

What Information Do Apps Collect?

When you install an app, it may ask for permissions: Camera, Microphone, Contacts, Location, Photos, and Bluetooth.

Some of these permissions make sense. A camera app needs your camera. Google Maps needs your location. WhatsApp needs access to your contacts if you want to find people you know.

But not every app needs access to everything. That is why you should actually check what permissions your apps have.

If a basic calculator app wants access to your microphone, location and contacts, that should make you ask: Why?

Can Your Phone See What You Search For?

Your search history can reveal your interests, problems, plans and questions.

Search for laptops and you have probably been researching laptops. Search for flights to Cape Town and there is a good chance you are thinking about travelling. Search for “how to fix my car” and your phone has another little piece of information about you.

One search might not mean much. But thousands of searches over months or years can create a surprisingly detailed picture of a person. And this is where things get interesting.

Is Your Phone Listening to You?

One of the biggest privacy questions people have is: “Is my phone listening to me?”

You have probably experienced this. You talk to someone about something, then later you see an advert related to it. It is easy to think: “There's no way that's a coincidence. My phone heard me.”

But targeted advertising does not necessarily require your phone to record your conversations. Companies can learn a lot from other data.

Your searches, websites, location, purchases, app activity, interests and the people or content you interact with can all help create a profile of you. So sometimes the technology looks like it is reading your mind when it is actually making a very educated guess. That is arguably even more interesting.

How Your Phone Learns Your Daily Habits

Modern smartphones are not just storing information. They can also recognise patterns.

For example, your phone might learn that you normally:

  • Wake up around 6:30
  • Leave home around 7:15
  • Spend the day at university or work
  • Use certain apps during lunch
  • Travel home in the afternoon
  • Watch YouTube at night
  • Charge your phone before going to sleep

None of these things individually seems very important. Put them together, and they describe your life surprisingly well.

This is one reason data is so valuable. A single piece of information can be boring. Millions of pieces of information can become a story.

How Social Media Tracks Your Behaviour

This is where things get even bigger.

Every time you like a post, watch a video, follow someone, search for something or spend time looking at a particular type of content, you are giving the platform information about your interests.

Even something as simple as watching a video until the end can be a signal. If you keep watching football videos but quickly scroll past cooking videos, the platform learns that you are probably more interested in football.

Do this thousands of times and the recommendations become extremely accurate. That is why TikTok, YouTube and Instagram can sometimes show you exactly what you want to see. They are not guessing randomly — they have data.

Why Do Companies Want Your Data?

Because information is useful.

Companies can use data to:

  • Personalise your experience
  • Recommend content
  • Show advertisements
  • Understand their users
  • Detect suspicious activity
  • Improve their products
  • Predict what users might want

For advertising companies, knowing what people are interested in can be extremely valuable.

An advertiser would rather show a laptop advert to someone searching for laptops than randomly show it to someone who has no interest in computers. Better targeting can mean better results.

So, How Much Does Your Phone Really Know About You?

Not exactly.

Your phone itself is just one part of a much bigger system. Your phone, apps, websites, social media platforms, advertising networks and online accounts can all collect different pieces of information.

The real issue is what happens when these pieces are combined:

  • Your location tells someone where you go.
  • Your searches show what you are interested in.
  • Your purchases show what you spend money on.
  • Your social media activity shows what content you like.
  • Your apps show what services you use.

Together, these things can create a detailed digital profile. And that profile can tell companies things about you that you may never have directly told them.

How to Stop Your Phone Tracking You

You don't have to throw your phone into the Vaal River and go live in the mountains.

There are simple, practical steps you can take to protect your privacy:

  • Check your app permissions regularly.
  • Turn off location access for apps that don't need it.
  • Delete apps you no longer use.
  • Review your Google and social media privacy settings.
  • Be careful about which apps you install.
  • Think before giving an app access to your contacts, microphone, camera or photos.

And remember that free apps are not always really “free”. Sometimes you are paying with your attention. Sometimes you are paying with your data.

The Weirdest Part: Connecting the Dots

The scary part isn't necessarily that your phone knows where you are. It's how much can be figured out from small pieces of information.

Your phone doesn't need to know everything about you. It just needs enough information to connect the dots. And once those dots are connected, your digital life can reveal a lot more about you than you might expect.

The next time your phone recommends something that feels way too accurate, remember: it probably isn't reading your mind. It has just been watching the patterns.

articles.title: 7 Tech Skills South African Companies Want in 2026
articles.content:
Tech is growing fast in South Africa, and companies need people who actually know how to use technology — not just people with certificates.

From software development and artificial intelligence to cybersecurity, cloud computing and data, tech skills are becoming increasingly important in South Africa's job market.

If you're a student, graduate or trying to get into tech, these are the skills worth learning right now.

1. Software Development

Coding is still one of the biggest tech skills.

Learn one language properly instead of trying to learn everything.

Good options:

  • Python
  • Java
  • JavaScript
  • TypeScript
  • C#

Then build actual projects. A GitHub full of projects is worth more than just saying “I know Python.”

2. Artificial Intelligence

AI is everywhere now.

If you want to go beyond just using ChatGPT, learn:

  • Python
  • Machine learning
  • APIs
  • Data
  • Generative AI

You don't have to build the next ChatGPT. Knowing how to use AI to build useful things is already a valuable skill.

3. Cybersecurity

More businesses are online, which means more systems need protecting.

Start with:

  • Networking
  • Linux
  • Operating systems
  • Security
  • Ethical hacking

Don't jump straight into “hacking”. Understand how the systems work first.

4. Cloud Computing

Companies are moving more of their systems to the cloud.

Learn one platform:

  • AWS
  • Azure
  • Google Cloud

Then add Linux, networking and DevOps.

5. Data

Businesses have tons of data. Someone has to make sense of it.

Learn:

  • SQL
  • Excel
  • Python
  • Power BI
  • Statistics

SQL is especially useful because almost every serious application has a database somewhere.

6. Web Development

Websites and web apps aren't going anywhere.

Start with:

HTML → CSS → JavaScript

Then move into things like React, Node.js or Next.js.

And actually build stuff. Don't spend six months watching tutorials.

7. AI + Programming

This one is becoming seriously important.

AI can already help developers write, debug and test code.

The skill isn't just knowing how to use AI. It's knowing when the AI is wrong.

Learn to use AI as a tool, while still understanding the code yourself.

So What Tech Skills in South Africa Should You Learn?

Here is an overview of the most in-demand tech roles in South Africa, essential tools to learn, and expected monthly earning potential:

Tech Skill Track Key Technologies & Tools Hiring Demand in SA Estimated Monthly Salary
Cloud & DevOps Engineering AWS, Azure, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform Critically High (Financial & Enterprise) R45,000 – R95,000 / month
Full-Stack Software Engineering TypeScript, React, Node.js, Python, PostgreSQL Consistently High across all sectors R35,000 – R85,000 / month
Cybersecurity Analysis Linux, Wireshark, SIEM, Firewalls, CompTIA Security+ High (Banks, Telecoms, Healthcare) R40,000 – R90,000 / month
Data Science & Engineering Python, SQL, PySpark, Power BI, Pandas Very High (Retail, Fintech, Insurance) R38,000 – R80,000 / month
AI Integration & Automation OpenAI API, LangChain, Python, Vector DBs Rapidly Growing in 2026 R42,000 – R95,000 / month

Don't try to learn everything.

  • Want to code? → Software development
  • Want AI? → Python + data + machine learning
  • Want cybersecurity? → Networking + Linux + security
  • Want cloud? → Linux + networking + AWS/Azure
  • Want data? → SQL + Python + Power BI

Pick one.

Learn it properly.

Build things.

Then learn the next one.

That's how you become useful in tech.
