articles.title: How to Pass Matric Maths Easily: 12 Tips That Actually Work
articles.content:
How to Pass Matric Maths Easily (Even If You’re Bad at Maths)

How to pass matric Maths? If you’re a high school student struggling with Mathematics, don’t skip this.

I have been a high school student too, and trust me, it wasn’t always easy for me.

For a long time, my problem wasn’t that I couldn’t do Mathematics. My problem was how I was studying it.

I used to study Maths like a subject where I could just read my notes, remember a few things and hope for the best in the exam.

That did not work.

Things started changing when I changed my perspective and, more importantly, my way of studying Mathematics.

I went from getting around 47% to 76% in my final exam.

So if you’re currently struggling with matric Maths, here are the things that helped me.

1. Stop reading Maths notes and start practising

This was probably the biggest change I made.

Maths is a practice subject.

You can read your textbook for three hours and still struggle when the actual question is in front of you.

Reading helps you understand the concept, but solving questions is what trains you to actually do Mathematics.

It’s okay to watch YouTube videos when you don’t understand something. But don’t make the mistake of watching someone solve 20 questions while you sit there thinking:

“Yeah, I understand this.”

Try this instead.

Watch the first example.

Pause the video.

Now take out your own paper and solve the question yourself.

After that, check your answer.

Then move on to the next example and try it yourself before watching the solution.

You’re not studying Maths by watching someone else do it.

You are studying Maths when you can do it yourself.

2. Start using past papers early

Don’t wait until three days before your Maths exam to suddenly download 10 past papers.

That’s panic, not preparation.

Start using past papers well before the exam.

Past papers can help you identify:

  • Topics you don’t understand
  • Question types you struggle with
  • Mistakes you keep making
  • How much time you spend on questions
  • Areas where you are losing marks

You can also use official NSC past papers and memos from the Department of Basic Education.

But don’t just do a past paper and check your percentage.

Study your mistakes.

If you got a question wrong, ask yourself:

Why did I get this wrong?

Was it because you didn’t know the formula?

Did you misunderstand the question?

Did you make an algebra mistake?

Did you use the wrong method?

That answer is more valuable than simply knowing that you got the question wrong.

3. Don’t cram Maths answers

Please don’t memorise an answer just because you saw it in a past paper.

You might get the exact same question.

But what happens when the numbers change?

You’re cooked.

Instead of memorising the answer, learn the method and the steps.

Ask yourself:

What type of question is this?

What method do I use?

What steps do I follow?

Once you understand the method, you can handle different versions of the same question.

That’s much more useful than memorising:

“The answer is 24.”

4. Learn how to use your formulas

Knowing that a formula exists isn’t enough.

You need to know:

  • What the formula is used for
  • When you should use it
  • What each variable means
  • How to substitute correctly
  • How to work through the calculation

Don’t just stare at the formula sheet.

Use the formulas.

Take different questions and practise identifying which formula you need.

Eventually, when you see a question, you should start thinking:

“Okay, this is the type of question where I need this formula.”

That is when formulas become useful.

5. Break Maths into smaller topics

One of the worst things you can tell yourself is:

“Today I’m going to study Maths.”

That’s too broad.

There are too many topics.

Instead, give yourself a specific target.

For example:

Monday: Functions

Tuesday: Finance

Wednesday: Trigonometry

Thursday: Analytical Geometry

Friday: Statistics

Now your brain has one specific job.

You don’t have to conquer the entire Maths syllabus in one sitting.

Break it down.

It’s much easier to say:

“Today I’m doing Functions.”

than:

“Today I’m doing Maths.”

6. Start with the topics you struggle with

Don’t spend your entire study session doing questions you already know because they make you feel good.

If you’re already getting 80% on Functions but 35% on Trigonometry, spending another five hours on Functions probably isn’t the best use of your time.

Find your weak areas.

Then attack them.

You don’t have to be perfect immediately.

Start with easier questions.

Understand the basics.

Then move to medium questions.

Then attempt harder ones.

Build your way up.

7. Learn how marks are awarded

This is something I wish more students understood.

In Mathematics, your working matters.

Don’t just write an answer and move on.

Show your calculations clearly.

If you make a mistake later in the question, your working can also help you understand where things went wrong.

When practising, get into the habit of showing your steps just like you would in the exam.

Don’t only practise getting the final answer.

Practise earning the marks.

8. Don’t leave the paper blank

Now, I’m not saying you should randomly write anything and expect the examiner to give you marks.

I’m saying don’t give up immediately when a question looks difficult.

Read it again.

Write down what you know.

Write down the relevant formula.

Look at the information given in the question.

Try to work out what the question is asking.

Start with something.

Sometimes the first step is enough to get you moving.

And if you genuinely don’t know how to continue, move on and come back later.

Don’t spend 20 minutes fighting one question while easier marks are waiting for you somewhere else.

9. Practise under time pressure

Being able to solve a Maths question is one thing.

Being able to solve it during an exam with a clock running is another thing.

When you start becoming comfortable with the topics, time yourself.

Do a section without constantly checking your phone or looking at the memo.

Eventually, try doing a full past paper under proper exam conditions.

Then check:

Did I finish?

Where did I waste time?

Which questions took too long?

Which questions did I rush?

The goal isn’t just to know Mathematics.

You also need to know how to manage your time.

10. Ask the smart students for help

This helped me too.

Sometimes your teacher explains something one way, but another student explains it in a way that suddenly makes everything click.

So don’t be afraid to ask someone who understands the topic.

Ask them:

“How did you get this answer?”

But don’t just copy their work.

Ask them to explain why they did each step.

Then try a similar question yourself.

If you can solve it without their help, you’ve actually learned something.

11. Go back and redo the questions you got wrong

This is one of the easiest ways to see whether you’re actually improving.

Let’s say you got five questions wrong today.

Don’t just look at the memo and forget about them.

Write down the questions you struggled with.

Come back a few days later.

Try them again without looking at the solution.

If you can now solve them, that’s progress.

If you still can’t, you know exactly what you need to work on.

Your mistakes can become your study guide.

12. Don’t try to learn everything the night before

We’ve all been there.

It’s 11 PM.

The exam is tomorrow.

Suddenly you decide you’re going to learn the entire Maths syllabus overnight.

Good luck.

Don’t do that.

Mathematics is much easier to improve when you practise consistently.

Even if you only have a limited amount of time, having a focused study session every day is better than trying to force the entire syllabus into your head the night before.

Small progress every day adds up.

The biggest lesson I learned

Going from 47% to 76% didn’t happen because I suddenly became a Mathematics genius.

I changed how I approached the subject.

I stopped treating Maths like something I could simply read.

I started practising.

I started using past papers.

I started paying attention to my mistakes.

I stopped memorising answers and started learning methods.

I broke the syllabus into smaller topics.

And I started asking for help when I didn’t understand something.

That’s what made the difference for me.

And finally… pray.

I’m not going to pretend studying is the only thing that matters.

If you’re a person of faith, pray.

Ask God for wisdom, discipline and understanding.

But don’t pray for the marks and then refuse to open the textbook.

Pray, then put in the work.

You don’t have to be the smartest person in your class to pass matric Maths.

You need a strategy, consistent practice and the willingness to learn from your mistakes.

You can improve.

Now go do some Maths.

Quick Matric Maths Checklist

Before your next exam, ask yourself:

  • Have I practised instead of only reading?
  • Have I used past papers?
  • Do I know my weak topics?
  • Have I redone questions I previously got wrong?
  • Do I know when to use my formulas?
  • Can I solve questions without looking at the memo?
  • Have I practised under time pressure?
  • Do I show all my working?
  • Have I asked for help where I’m stuck?
  • Have I actually put in the work?

Don’t just study harder. Study smarter.

articles.title: Chinese Cars in South Africa: Why Are They So Popular in 2026?
articles.content:
I have noticed something mind-boggling on South African roads lately.

Chinese cars.

A few years ago, seeing a Chinese car on South African roads felt like having a foreign tourist come to your village and everyone just stares awkwardly.

Now?

They are impossible to ignore.

BYD. Chery. GWM. Haval. Omoda. Jaecoo. Jetour.

You see them everywhere.

And this isn’t just me imagining things. Chinese brands have been growing rapidly in South Africa. Their share of the passenger-car market increased from 11.2% in 2024 to 16.8% in 2025. By the first quarter of 2026, Chinese brands were approaching a fifth of the local new-vehicle market. (TimesLIVE)

So why the sudden increase?

You Get More For Your Money

This is probably one of the biggest reasons.

Chinese cars are coming packed with features.

I’m talking about bigger screens, cameras, sunroofs, driver-assistance technology, electric windows, electric boots and a whole list of other features.

And sometimes you look at the price and think:

“Wait, that’s all included?”

You can look at some well-established brands and find a fairly basic car at a similar price, while some Chinese competitors are giving you a much longer list of features.

Want the bigger screen?

It’s there.

Want cameras?

There.

Want a sunroof?

Sometimes, it’s there too.

And when you start adding those kinds of features to other cars, the price can climb very quickly.

That’s what makes Chinese cars so interesting to me.

They are giving people a lot of car for their money.

And clearly, South African buyers are noticing.

The Quality Has Changed

Let’s be honest.

Chinese cars didn’t always have the reputation they have today.

But things have changed.

Look at some of the newer Chinese cars and they genuinely look good.

The interiors look modern. The screens look good. The materials feel better and the overall build quality seems much more polished than what many people remember.

I’m still not the biggest fan of some of the body lines though.

Some of them are just doing a little too much for me.

But the interiors?

Nice.

The build quality?

Definitely better than what I remember from years ago.

And this is probably one of the biggest reasons people are starting to take these cars seriously.

They don’t feel like they are trying to compete only on price anymore.

Chinese Cars Are Going Crazy With Technology

Technology might be their secret weapon.

Infotainment screens, driver assistance, cameras, hybrid systems, electric vehicles and fuel-efficient engines are becoming major selling points.

And let’s not even get started on the safety technology.

Some of these cars have so many cameras and sensors that it feels like the car knows what is happening around you before you do.

That technology also changes the driving experience.

They feel easy to drive because the car is constantly helping you.

It almost feels like you’re driving a computer that happens to have four wheels.

And this isn’t just a small trend either. Plug-in hybrid sales in South Africa jumped dramatically in 2025, with Chinese brands helping drive the growth of more affordable plug-in hybrid models. (CleanTechnica)

Then There Are The Crazy Car Tests

This is another thing I find interesting.

I’ve seen videos of Chinese manufacturers putting their cars through some seriously crazy tests.

Crash tests.

Water tests.

Extreme manoeuvres.

Tests designed to show what these cars can actually handle.

I even recently saw a video of a car performing what looked like a barrel roll in a tunnel.

I just sat there thinking:

“Why are they doing this?”

But at the same time…

That’s pretty cool.

And I think that’s part of the appeal.

Chinese manufacturers aren’t just saying:

“Our car is affordable.”

They’re also trying to show people:

“Look what this thing can do.”

Obviously, one crazy demonstration doesn’t prove that every Chinese car is going to last 20 years without a problem.

But it definitely gets people’s attention.

But I’m Not Saying Chinese Cars Are Better

Let’s make that clear.

I’m not saying Chinese cars are automatically better than Toyota, Volkswagen, Ford or any other established brand.

They still have things to prove.

Reliability over many years matters.

Resale value matters.

Parts availability matters.

After-sales support matters.

Established brands have spent decades building trust with South African drivers.

Chinese brands are still building that trust.

But I think it would be a mistake to ignore them.

The numbers are already showing that South Africans are giving them a chance. In the first half of 2026, several Chinese brands recorded strong sales growth, while brands such as Chery, Jetour and GWM continued climbing the local rankings. (TopAuto)

And that’s the part I find most interesting.

Would I Buy One?

If I had to get one myself right now?

The BYD Shark 6.

That thing is beautiful.

I’ve seen it and honestly, it is one of those cars that makes you stop and look.

And that’s probably the biggest change of all.

A few years ago, many South Africans would see a Chinese car and ask:

“What is that?”

Now people are asking:

“How much is it?”

That’s a big difference.

Chinese cars aren’t some strange new thing on South African roads anymore.

They’re becoming a serious part of the market.

articles.title: AI in South Africa: Should We Fear What AI Will Take Away?
articles.content:
Are you looking for detailed information and insights about AI in South Africa? Read on to find out more.

Will AI Really Change the Industry?

Will AI really change the industry?

In South Africa, I am still skeptical about how quickly this will happen. I feel like we are still experiencing slow development compared to other parts of the world.

But at the same time, a lot of people are scared of AI.

The Race Is About Who Uses AI Best

I always tell people to use every obstacle as a stepping stone. Right now, we shouldn’t be afraid of what AI threatens. We should find a way to use it to the best of our abilities.

We might be entering a race of who can use AI the best.

If you can use AI to build working projects that solve real-world problems, I believe you are starting to master it and are on the right path.

There are people using AI as diaries or whatever(not very useful things), and there are people using AI almost like an employee to help them build or tutor to help them learn. These people are different. They simply have the same tool but use it differently.

I Learned by Building With AI

I can attest to this myself.

I am 20 years old, and I have built successful websites and automation systems. At first, all I had was ChatGPT. Then I was introduced to Gemini and other AI tools, and it went further from there.

What helped me most was research. I wanted to understand what these models could actually do, so I kept testing them and learning their capabilities. Bit by bit, I learned how to use AI to build real projects.

AI Is More Than Copy and Paste

And I am not talking about AI-generated copy-and-paste slop.

I mean using AI through the entire development process:

  • Researching a problem
  • Designing a solution
  • Writing code
  • Debugging
  • Testing
  • Improving the product
  • Deploying it
  • Getting feedback
  • Repeating the process until the project works

The Real Value of AI lies on how you use it.

Today, I am not even ashamed of my CV. In fact, I am proud of what I have been able to build with the tools available to me.

I urge everyone reading this to not see AI as the enemy, but as the tool that will improve our productivity.

articles.title: No Man, Why Is Petrol So Expensive? Here’s Why
articles.content:
Are you looking for detailed information and insights about why is petrol so expensive in South Africa? Read on to find out more.

Have you ever sat and wondered why petrol prices actually increase and who actually determines the price?

I am a new driver myself, and it still shocks me how much I spend on fuel every week just doing my daily commutes to University and back home. But while I was pouring petrol recently, I thought, no man, why is this so expensive?

Is it because of the tedious process of making fuel?

Not mainly.

Why does petrol get more expensive?

South Africa’s fuel prices are influenced by a few major things.

International Fuel Prices

South Africa is affected by what happens in the international fuel market. When international oil and refined fuel prices go up, South Africa can also end up paying more for fuel.

The Rand and the Dollar

Fuel is traded internationally in US dollars. So when the rand weakens, we need more rands to buy the same amount of fuel.

Taxes and Other Costs

The price also includes government taxes and levies, as well as costs involved in shipping, storing, transporting and selling the fuel.

So who actually determines the price?

South Africa uses a regulated fuel pricing system. The monthly price adjustment is announced by the Minister of Mineral and Petroleum Resources based on the regulated pricing formula. They are not simply choosing a price out of nowhere. The formula takes international prices, the exchange rate and local costs into account.

Does Making Fuel Affect the Price?

And yes, making and refining fuel does cost money, but it is only one part of the bigger picture.

Can South Africa make its own petrol?

South Africa does make and refine some of its own fuel, but we simply don’t produce enough to meet all our needs. So we also rely on imported crude oil and finished fuel, which means what happens to international fuel prices still affects us.

Basically, it is a chain reaction. Something happens internationally, the exchange rate moves, costs change, and eventually we feel it at the petrol station, yea no.

articles.title: Matriculants 2026: Apply for NSFAS, But Don't Ignore Other Bursaries
articles.content:
If you are a matriculant hoping to study after Grade 12, apply for NSFAS if you qualify. But don’t stop there.

Table of Contents

  • Don’t depend on one bursary
  • What worked for me
  • Start now for bursaries
  • Where to look for bursaries
  • The finish line is near

I’m saying this as a university student to someone who is about to enter university. I have seen for myself what studying hard and applying for opportunities can do.

There are many private bursaries, company bursaries and university funding opportunities available. If you qualify, apply.

Don’t depend on one bursary

NSFAS is important and helps many students get through university. But it has also faced challenges with funding and administration.

So why put all your hopes on one funding option?

Apply for private bursaries too. Some can help with tuition, accommodation, books, meals and other study costs. Some may also offer laptops, mentorship, internships or other opportunities.

What worked for me

I made it my goal to apply for almost every bursary I qualified for.

Sometimes I applied for two or three in one day.

I got rejected many times. But I kept going.

You don’t need every bursary to say yes. You only need a few to say yes.

I also took my studies seriously and learned to manage my time. There were many nights when I had to study while also looking for bursaries and completing applications.

But it paid off.

The university life I am living now is something I honestly did not think I would experience this soon. I have been able to get things I used to dream about, including laptops and phones.

That experience taught me one thing: put yourself in as many opportunities as possible.

Start now for bursaries

Don’t wait until January.

Look for bursaries now, check their requirements and apply before they close. Closing dates change, so always check the official website of the funder.

Keep your important documents ready, including your ID, latest results and proof of income.

And don’t be scared of rejection. I got plenty of them.

A bursary you never apply for can never accept you.

Where to look for bursaries

  • NSFAS for government funding
  • ISFAP for missing-middle funding
  • StudyTrust for different bursary opportunities
  • ZABursaries for bursary listings
  • AllBursaries for more opportunities
  • FundiConnect for funding information

Always check that the bursary is legitimate before sending your personal documents.

Never pay someone simply because they promise to get you a bursary. If something looks suspicious, check the organisation’s official website first.

The finish line is near

If you’re writing matric this year, you still have this.

Study hard. Manage your time. Apply for NSFAS if you qualify, but also apply for private and company bursaries.

You will get rejected. I did too.

But you only need a few doors to open.

Keep applying. Keep studying. The finish line is near.

articles.title: Eskom Data Centres: It Has Power to Spare. Now It Wants Amazon, Microsoft and Google to Buy It
articles.content:
Eskom is talking to Amazon, Microsoft and Google about selling them electricity. The idea is to power the data centres these companies use to run things like cloud storage and AI. Providing power to these Eskom data centres clients is a new priority.

Eskom's chairperson, Mteto Nyati confirmed the talks in an interview with the Financial Times, published on 12 August 2026, about having discussions with Amazon, Microsoft & Google.

Nothing has been signed or confirmed yet. As of 18 August, there's no confirmed deal - just ongoing talks.

Why does Eskom suddenly have extra power to sell? Why?

For the past years, South Africa had power cuts almost every single day aka load-shedding. That's now over. The country hasn't had load-shedding for more than a year.

Eskom fixed a lot of problems with its power plants, so fewer breakdowns happen. This means more electricity is available than before. Right now, Eskom has about 6 gigawatts (GW) of extra power at peak times - the most spare capacity it's had in almost 10 years.

In simple terms: Eskom is now making more electricity than the country is using.

Eskom data centres: Why the sudden push?

Data centres are large facilities packed with computer servers. They use huge amounts of electricity, especially in these times of AI. So they're an obvious customer for Eskom with spare or leftover electricity to sell.

South Africa already has about 70% of all the data centre capacity on the entire African continent. That’s huge numbers. The data/AI industry is expected double in size by 2031.

Not everyone agrees this will work

Here's the catch. South Africa's biggest data centre company, Teraco, says power supply isn't actually the industry's main problem.

According to Teraco, what data centres really struggle with is getting connected to the power grid, and getting access to renewable energy like solar and wind - not a shortage of electricity to buy.

This matters because big tech companies like Amazon, Google and Microsoft usually want to run on renewable energy, not power made mostly from burning coal, which is how most of Eskom's electricity is produced. So even if Eskom has plenty of power, these companies might not want that specific kind of power.

Some data centre operators are already building their own renewable power sources instead. Teraco, for example, is building its own 120 megawatt solar plant and has a separate deal to buy wind power.

Eskom still has money problems

Even with extra power to sell, Eskom is far from financially healthy.

  • Eskom owes about R359 billion in debt, even after the government gave it a R254 billion bailout.


  • Municipalities across the country owe Eskom around R118 billion in unpaid electricity bills.

Selling power to data centres could bring in useful extra income, but it won't fix these bigger financial problems on its own.

What to watch next

Right now, this is just talk - no contracts have been signed. What happens next depends on things like:

  • Whether Eskom can offer competitive prices


  • Whether these companies are willing to use coal-based power, even partly


  • Whether Eskom can actually connect data centres to the grid where they need it

We'll update this article if any of the three companies confirm a deal, or if Eskom shares more details.

articles.title: Springboks vs All Blacks: THE BIG GAME
articles.content:
The most loved by South Africans Springboks face the All Blacks at Ellis Park in Johannesburg on Saturday, 22 August 2026. Kick-off is at 17:10 SAST. It's the first Test of Rugby's Greatest Rivalry, a new four-Test series between the two teams.

Springboks vs All Blacks: When will the team be announced?

Coach Rassie Erasmus will only name his starting team on Thursday, 20 August — later than his usual pattern this year of naming the team on a Monday or Tuesday. Erasmus said the delay is deliberate, to limit the All Blacks' preparation time — a mark of respect for New Zealand, he said, not arrogance.

Kolisi and Nche fitness update

Captain Siya Kolisi (hamstring) and prop Ox Nche (knee) are the only two players Erasmus has flagged as doubtful for Saturday. Erasmus described their issues as niggles rather than injuries, and said both could still play if they get through this week's training.

If Kolisi isn't available, Pieter-Steph du Toit is reported to be the likely stand-in captain. This hasn't been confirmed by Erasmus — it's early reporting from a single source, so treat it as speculation until Thursday's announcement.

How the All Blacks have been playing

Before this Test, the All Blacks played three provincial matches in South Africa, winning all three by big margins:

  • Beat the Stormers 38-21 (7 August)


  • Beat the Sharks 54-0 (11 August)


  • Beat the Bulls 50-19 (15 August)

The bigger picture

This tour replaces the usual Rugby Championship for 2026. It's the first time the All Blacks have toured South Africa for a full series in around 30 years. After Ellis Park, the teams meet three more times: at DHL Stadium in Cape Town (29 August), FNB Stadium in Johannesburg (5 September), and in Baltimore, USA (12 September). The Springboks will tour New Zealand in return in 2030.

Tickets for the main Test venues, including Ellis Park, are reported sold out.

What we don't know yet

The final Springboks team, the starting captain, and whether Kolisi and Nche will be fit are all still unknown. That will only be confirmed on Thursday, 20 August.

articles.title: MTN Launches AI Job Board for African Youth
articles.content:
MTN Group launched an AI-powered Job Board on 12 August 2026 as part of its free MTN Skills Academy. The feature connects job discovery with skills development and application tracking and is available across the 11 MTN markets where the Skills Academy operates. The launch happened on International Youth Day.

  • What the MTN AI Job Board Does
  • How to access the MTN AI Job Board
  • Where it's available
  • The numbers behind it
  • Why MTN is doing this
  • Built for accessibility
  • What we still don't know

What the MTN AI Job Board Does

According to MTN, the Job Board recommends job opportunities based on a learner's skills, location and career goals. Users can filter and save vacancies, track their applications, and get recommendations for free Skills Academy courses to close any skills gaps for the roles they want.

How to access the MTN AI Job Board

  1. Go to skillsacademy.mtn.com
  2. Sign in to the MTN Skills Academy or create an account
  3. Open the Jobs section available through the platform
  4. Browse vacancies recommended based on your skills, location and career goals
  5. Filter and save relevant vacancies
  6. Track your application progress through the platform
  7. Where you have a skills gap, check the free Skills Academy courses recommended for the role

Where it's available

MTN confirms the Job Board is available across all 11 MTN Skills Academy markets. ITWeb specifically names South Africa, Uganda, Zambia, Rwanda, and Ghana, but MTN's release does not provide an itemised list of all 11.

The numbers behind it

MTN says its Skills Academy has, since launching in 2022:

  • Nearly 526,000 enrolments
  • 192,000 course completions
  • 1,122 specialisations completed

These are MTN-reported figures and haven't been independently audited.

MTN also cites a projection from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) that more than 230 million jobs in sub-Saharan Africa will need digital skills by 2030.

Why MTN is doing this

Marina Madale, MTN Group's Executive for Sustainability and Shared Value, said the Job Board is a way of putting the company's commitment to digital and economic inclusion into practice by connecting learning, skills, and job opportunities. She also said turning skills into real jobs takes effort from business, government, and educators together.

Built for accessibility

The Skills Academy platform includes accessibility features for users with visual, cognitive, neurological, mobility, and age-related needs. Anyone who finishes a course gets a digital certificate.

What we still don't know

MTN hasn't said how many jobs were listed on the Job Board at launch, who the employers are, or named all 11 markets individually. There's also no data yet on how many people have used the tool since it went live.

articles.title: SADC Summit 2026: Ramaphosa Takes Over as Chair in Durban
articles.content:
Leaders from the Southern African Development Community (SADC) are meeting in Durban today, 17 August 2026, for the 46th Ordinary Summit. President Cyril Ramaphosa is hosting the event at the Inkosi Albert Luthuli International Convention Centre.

  • Ramaphosa becomes SADC Chair
  • Who is attending
  • What's on the agenda
  • Security tightened in Durban
  • What happens next
  • Sources

Ramaphosa becomes SADC Chair

South Africa is formally assuming the SADC Chairpersonship for 2026/27, with President Cyril Ramaphosa taking over as the bloc's Chairperson. Ramaphosa has been serving as interim chair since November 2025, after Madagascar relinquished the position amid a political crisis in that country.

Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema currently holds the role of Interim Incoming Chairperson and Deputy Chairperson of SADC.

Who is attending

Nine heads of state are reported to be attending in person, while other member states are represented by government delegations.

What's on the agenda

This year's summit theme is: "Resilient, sustainable and inclusive industrialisation through Infrastructure Development, Agricultural and Critical Minerals Transformation in Pursuit of a Just World." In simple terms, leaders are focused on growing the region through better infrastructure, farming, and the use of critical minerals.

Other issues expected to come up include:

  • Migration and the free movement of people are also expected to feature in discussions. South Africa has been pushing for progress on the region's stalled free-movement framework. Recent reports indicate that Zimbabwe and Mozambique have opposed bringing the issue directly before summit leaders.
  • The security situation in eastern DRC
  • Madagascar's political crisis and its path back to elections

No final decisions or an official closing communiqué have been released yet.

Security tightened in Durban

Security was tightened around the summit venue after three people were detained in connection with access-control incidents. Two Congolese nationals were arrested for allegedly trying to enter the venue using accreditation issued to other people, while a Zimbabwean national was arrested earlier after allegedly trying to obtain accreditation by posing as a performing artist.

A protest march is also planned in Durban today. Police say people have the right to protest, but it must not disrupt the summit.

What happens next

SADC is expected to release an official summary of the summit's decisions once it ends. This article will be updated once that happens.

What happens to the content

MultiChoice says the programming from all four closing channels will still be available on DStv, just spread across other channels instead of having a dedicated slot. The company hasn't said exactly where each show or movie is moving to, and it isn't clear yet whether M-Net Movies 1 content specifically ends up on the renamed M Movies+ channel or elsewhere.

If you regularly watch something on one of these four channels, the safest move is to check the DStv channel guide or app closer to 16 September rather than assuming it lands in the same place.

Why is MultiChoice cutting these channels?

MultiChoice's explanation, given in a statement reported by several South African outlets, is that it's consolidating similar content onto fewer, stronger channels rather than spreading it thin across many. The company frames this as a cleaner, easier line-up for subscribers to navigate.

That explanation sits inside a bigger shift. Groupe Canal+ took full control of MultiChoice Group in September 2025. Since then, MultiChoice SA LicenceCo, the locally licensed entity that actually runs DStv in South Africa, has been the one confirming these changes, a structure required to meet South African ownership rules for broadcasters. Under Canal+, the company has leaned harder into cost control and growing its cheaper packages, while Premium has been the tier absorbing most of the cuts.

SuperSport is changing too, from 19 August 2026

The September channel closures aren't happening in isolation. A separate reshuffle of SuperSport channels is set to take effect from 19 August 2026, about a month before the Premium channel closures:

  • SuperSport Football Plus, carrying premium football including selected UEFA Champions League matches
  • SuperSport Africa
  • SuperSport KickOff
  • SuperSport Extra 2

Some reports also mention an added SportyTV channel around the same time. Coverage of this reshuffle has generally described it as new channels and a reorganisation of sport, rather than a cut, unlike the September closures.

Part of a longer 2026 pattern for DStv Premium

The September closures are the latest in a run of changes that have hit DStv Premium through 2026:

  • January 2026: BET Africa, MTV Base, CBS Reality and CBS Justice were removed as Paramount wound down its African linear channels.
  • Late January 2026: Tlnovelas was removed. It was replaced by Novelas+ on 1 July 2026.
  • 30 April 2026: Showmax, which had been a free add-on for Premium subscribers, shut down. Some of its content moved to DStv Stream.
  • Late June 2026: CineMagic and Magic Showcase closed. Around the same time, MultiChoice confirmed that first-run HBO and Warner Bros. Discovery shows, including House of the Dragon, were no longer available on M-Net or its Catch Up service, due to studio licensing and distribution agreements following the Canal+ takeover.
  • 16 September 2026: M-Net Movies 1, kykNET Lekker, Mzansi Bioskop and Mzansi Music close.

Adding the four January Paramount channels to the four closing in September, some outlets, including Legit.ng, describe Premium as having lost seven channels over the course of 2026. That's an accurate running total, but it wasn't announced as a single event. It's a count built by combining two separate rounds of cuts.

Counting every discontinued DStv channel in 2026, including ones that were later replaced, some reports put the total at 11. Others count 9, depending on whether replacement channels and earlier removals are included. There's no single official MultiChoice figure for this, so treat any specific total as an estimate rather than a confirmed number.

Is DStv Premium still worth it after these cuts?

That's the question a lot of subscribers are asking, and there isn't a clean yes or no answer from MultiChoice. What's measurable is this: according to MyBroadband's tracking, Premium hasn't gained a single new channel in 2026 so far, while the cheaper Access package has picked up WWE, Trace channels and full live coverage of the FIFA World Cup, the first time Access has offered World Cup coverage at that scale.

MyBroadband's decade comparison also shows the Premium package growing only slightly on paper, from 139 channels in 2016 to 141 in mid-2026, while its satellite price rose from R759 to R979 over the same period, a 29% increase. Premium subscriber numbers have fallen from around 2.1 million to around 1 million over the same decade. MultiChoice hasn't announced any DStv price increases for 2026, so the current cuts aren't paired with a price hike, at least for now.

Whether that adds up to Premium losing value is a judgement call for each household, based on what you actually watch. If your viewing leans heavily on general entertainment, sport highlights and international content rather than the specific channels closing, the day-to-day change may be minor. If you rely on kykNET Lekker, Mzansi Bioskop or Mzansi Music specifically, it's a bigger loss, especially since it isn't yet clear exactly where that content resurfaces.

articles.title: Colombia Earthquake 2026: What We Know So Far
articles.content:
The quake struck near San José del Palmar in Chocó department at about 07:34 local time (12:34 UTC). The U.S. Geological Survey recorded a magnitude of 7.4 and a depth of roughly 107 kilometres, with the epicentre a few kilometres from San José del Palmar.

Strong shaking was reported across western and central parts of the country, including Cali, Pereira, Medellín and Bogotá, with tremors also felt beyond Colombia's borders. The hardest-hit areas included parts of the country's coffee-growing region.

Casualties and damage – Colombia earthquake 2026

As of 12 August, Reuters reported at least 254 deaths, while more than 2,500 injuries were reported. Rescue teams were still searching damaged buildings and other sites as authorities continued assessing the scale of the disaster. The figures may change as reports from affected areas are consolidated.

Buildings were damaged or destroyed in several affected communities, while homes and public infrastructure were also hit. Airports carried out safety checks and some facilities, including hospitals and schools, were affected by the earthquake.

Rescue and emergency response

Colombia's president declared a national emergency as the extent of the damage became clearer. Emergency services and search-and-rescue teams were mobilised, with rescue crews, soldiers, specialist personnel, volunteers and trained dogs involved in searches through collapsed structures; some survivors were pulled from the rubble.

Humanitarian and emergency assistance is being coordinated as rescue and recovery operations continue.

Aftershocks have continued following the main earthquake. Readers should rely on updates from Colombia's Servicio Geológico Colombiano and other official seismic monitoring agencies for the latest information on aftershocks and seismic activity.

Related News: 46th SADC Summit: Ramaphosa Takes Over as Chair in Durban

Current situation and what happens next

Rescue operations remain the immediate priority, particularly in areas where access and communications have been disrupted. Damage assessments are still incomplete, especially in more remote parts of Chocó and other affected regions.

The situation remains fluid. Death and injury figures, the number of people still unaccounted for and the extent of infrastructure damage can change as rescue teams reach more locations and authorities consolidate reports.

Authorities are expected to focus on locating survivors, treating the injured, restoring access to affected communities and assessing damaged buildings and infrastructure. For residents and families affected by the earthquake, information from official emergency and seismic agencies remains the most reliable source as conditions develop.

Readers following the Colombia earthquake 2026 should check the latest updates from Colombian authorities, the Servicio Geológico Colombiano, the USGS and established international news organisations.

articles.title: TS Galaxy 2-3 Mamelodi Sundowns: Mkhulise late brace ends Mbombela hoodoo
articles.content:
TS Galaxy 2-3 Mamelodi Sundowns: Mkhulise late brace ends Mbombela hoodoo

Mamelodi Sundowns began their 2026/27 Betway Premiership campaign with a remarkable 3-2 comeback against TS Galaxy at Mbombela Stadium on Tuesday, 11 August 2026.

Galaxy were leading 2-1 with the match entering its final stages, but substitute Sphelele Mkhulise scored twice to turn the game in Sundowns' favour.

The victory also ended Sundowns' recent struggle to beat Galaxy in Mpumalanga.

TS Galaxy 2-3 Mamelodi Sundowns

MinuteScorerTeam
7'Brayan León (penalty)Mamelodi Sundowns
33'Victor LetsoaloTS Galaxy
77'Victor Letsoalo*TS Galaxy
88'/89'Sphelele MkhuliseMamelodi Sundowns
Stoppage timeSphelele MkhuliseMamelodi Sundowns

*The official PSL statistical record lists the 77th-minute goal as a Ronwen Williams own goal, while the club and several media reports credit it to Victor Letsoalo. The match narrative here follows the latter convention.

How Sundowns turned the game around

Sundowns got on the scoreboard early when Tashreeq Matthews was brought down inside the penalty area. Brayan León took responsibility from the spot and sent the goalkeeper the wrong way to make it 1-0.

Galaxy gradually found their way back into the contest. Their equaliser arrived in the 33rd minute when Victor Letsoalo finished after Sundowns were caught out following a loss of possession.

The home team then completed the turnaround after the break. A Mpho Mvelase free-kick created the opportunity for Letsoalo, whose header ended up in the goal after Ronwen Williams was unable to keep the ball out.

Sundowns were suddenly facing another disappointing result at a ground where they had struggled in recent meetings with Galaxy.

Miguel Cardoso responded from the bench, bringing on Sphelele Mkhulise.

The change proved decisive.

Mkhulise pulled Sundowns level late in the match. His effort took a deflection before finding the net, giving the visitors renewed belief.

There was still time for one more twist.

Khuliso Mudau played a part in the winning move, with Mkhulise finishing again in stoppage time to complete his brace and send Sundowns home with all three points.

The match was played in wet and cold conditions, adding to the difficulty of the contest.

Mkhulise becomes the difference

Mkhulise was not on the pitch when Galaxy established their 2-1 advantage.

By the final whistle, he was the main reason Sundowns had won.

The football midfielder's introduction gave Cardoso's side an attacking spark when they needed it most. His two late finishes transformed a match that appeared to be slipping away into a winning start to the league campaign.

For Sundowns, it was an early example of the depth available within the squad.

León gives Sundowns the perfect start

Before Mkhulise's late heroics, León had given Sundowns the advantage from the penalty spot.

The Colombian forward joined the club from Independiente Medellín in January 2026 and made an impact during the second half of the previous campaign.

His early goal at Mbombela gave Sundowns control of the opening stages, although Galaxy eventually turned the match around.

Why the Mbombela win matters

The venue added extra significance to the result.

Galaxy had beaten Sundowns 3-2 at the same stadium in May 2026. That defeat came during the final stages of the previous league campaign and hurt Sundowns' title challenge.

This time, Sundowns produced the opposite result.

They had failed to win on their previous four visits to Mpumalanga to face Galaxy. Breaking that run required a comeback after conceding twice, making the victory even more dramatic.

There was also a notable season-opening record on the line.

Sundowns are now unbeaten in 19 consecutive league season openers, with 13 wins and six draws since their last opening-day defeat in 2007.

What else happened in the Betway Premiership?

Three other league matches were played on 11 August:

  • Polokwane City 3-3 Stellenbosch FC
  • Chippa United 1-1 Richards Bay
  • Marumo Gallants 0-0 Kruger United

The early league table remains unsettled because clubs have played different numbers of matches.

What's next for Sundowns?

Sundowns now turn their attention to Kaizer Chiefs.

The two sides meet at FNB Stadium on Saturday, 15 August 2026, giving Sundowns only a few days to recover from their dramatic win in Mbombela.

The match will provide an early test of whether Sundowns can carry their winning momentum into the new campaign.

What the result means

Sundowns looked set to leave Mbombela empty-handed after Galaxy took a 2-1 lead in the second half.

Instead, two late goals from Mkhulise changed everything.

The comeback gives Sundowns three points to begin the new Betway Premiership season and, perhaps just as importantly, ends a difficult recent run against Galaxy in Mpumalanga.

For Galaxy, the defeat will be particularly frustrating after holding the lead so late in the match.

For Sundowns, the focus now moves to their next challenge against Kaizer Chiefs.
